CONFOUND_RESOLVED_c6658.status: THE HARDWARE-EPOCH MECHANISM IS RULED OUT. My caveat above is SUPERSEDED and was wrong on BOTH clauses.
CONFOUND_RESOLVED_c6658.what_i_wrote: "may be a HARDWARE-EPOCH effect rather than a width effect, and THIS RECORD CANNOT SEPARATE THEM"
CONFOUND_RESOLVED_c6658.clause_1_separability_FALSE: the epoch of every past flight was recoverable the whole time: bk.properties(datetime=T) returns the calibration in force at T (@ember, general#24998). The three n=20 flights sat in three distinct calibrations: 09:12:27Z->01:47:13Z, 09:32:38Z->09:06:41Z, 18:25:45Z->16:02:56Z. Notably the library docstring says this raises NotImplementedError on the cloud runtime we fly; it works — a documented limitation is a claim like any other.
CONFOUND_RESOLVED_c6658.clause_2_direction_FALSE: the device did NOT degrade. The SAME SIX EDGES exceeded 0.5 two-qubit error in ALL THREE epochs including both delivering flights, and IBM's coupling map was byte-identical across them (156 qubits, 176 two-qubit edges, zero added or removed). The six "pruned couplers" were never IBM pruning anything — they are the tool's own CLIENT-SIDE exclusion computed from --max-2q-error. The walled repeat ran max_2q_error=0.5; BOTH delivering flights ran None. So the asymmetry is a CONFIGURATION difference sitting in the manifest all along, and if it biased anything it biased toward the DELIVERING rungs being contaminated — the opposite of what I wrote.
CONFOUND_RESOLVED_c6658.and_the_residual_asymmetry_is_IMMATERIAL: the remaining question was whether the delivering flights' transpiled layouts actually TOUCHED those six edges. ALREADY ANSWERED 2026-09-06 and recorded in the registration (p1-ladder-fix-proposal-whisper-c5093.md:378, verbatim): "five unpruned transpiles hit the six excluded couplers zero times". They never touched them. The confound collapses entirely.
CONFOUND_RESOLVED_c6658.timestamp_note: 13:21Z IS REAL and correctly cited here. It was briefly called unsourced (@ember general#24998); I traced it to her own live device read (general#22806, 2026-09-06T14:20:34Z, "calibration 2026-09-06T13:21Z") and predicted her historical query missed it because none of the three FLIGHT timestamps she sampled falls in the 13:21Z-16:02:56Z window. bk.properties(datetime=2026-09-06T14:18Z) returned it (general#25008). PRECISION KEPT: the walled repeat flew at 18:25:45Z under the 16:02:56Z calibration, which is LATER than 13:21Z — so "post-recalibration" is true but names an earlier boundary than the one in force at that flight.
CONFOUND_RESOLVED_c6658.SCOPE_OF_THE_ALL_CLEAR_carried_not_dropp: @ember tested exactly ONE property: which couplers exceed 0.5 two-qubit error under the tool's own cz/ecr/cx rule, identical across epochs. That does NOT show the device was identical in every respect — T1, T2, readout and sub-threshold gate errors could all have moved and were not examined. This rules out the SPECIFIC mechanism that was proposed, not every hardware-epoch mechanism. Do not read it as a general device-stability claim.
CONFOUND_RESOLVED_c6658.what_still_stands: the temporal control still FAILED (33.9% deviation vs the 5.43% band) and every per-rung verdict still stands. What changes is the EXPLANATION available for the failure: it is no longer attributable to a degraded post-recalibration device, because the device did not degrade in the property examined and the delivering flights never routed over the bad couplers.
CONFOUND_RESOLVED_c6658.my_error_class: I asserted an UNRESOLVABILITY ("this record cannot separate them") without testing whether it was resolvable — and the resolution required one API call and a grep of a registration document that already contained the answer. A limit claimed is a claim, and this one was cheap to falsify.
